title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
authors: Liuyi Xu, Yun Guo, Shusheng Li, Xuewen Zhang, Yining Qian, An-Yang Lu
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.

infographic.key_insight: OmniTongue exposes substantial gaps in multimodal AI’s ability to interpret fine-grained tongue features in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM).
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark supports research on automated TCM tongue assessment but does not establish clinical diagnostic validity or readiness.
method: Constructed a visual question-answering benchmark from expert-validated tongue images.
Covered 16 clinical dimensions and 66 fine-grained labels.
Added region-specific annotations to evaluate feature localization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation using 1,351 images and 21,616 instruction pairs found no domain advantage for medical-specific models and broadly poor Macro-F1 scores.
infographic.watch_item: Poor Macro-F1 scores raise concerns about statistical shortcuts, and the abstract provides no evidence of prospective clinical validation.

title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
authors: Pau Mateo-Bernadó, Saivenkata Nagavyjayanthi Polapragada, David Bonet, Pol Arbiol Rakuljic, Laia Mogas Pladevall, Marçal Comajoan Cara
abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

infographic.key_insight: Tabular foundation models perform best as a family, but tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain competitive depending on the dataset and compute budget.
infographic.clinical_relevance: TabBioMed can inform model selection for biomedical prediction research, but the abstract does not establish clinical readiness or patient benefit.
method: Curate 94 public biomedical tabular datasets across eight domains.
Standardize dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation for classification, regression, and multi-target tasks.
Compare 23 models spanning classical baselines, boosted trees, neural architectures, and tabular foundation models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 94 datasets and 23 models, predictive performance and computational trade-offs varied by data regime and task type.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark leaders may not suit every deployment: model choice should account for dataset characteristics, training cost, and inference constraints.
infographic.paper_title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning

title: LabARIA: A Multi-Agent System for Integrative Analytics in Clinical Laboratories
authors: Li, H.; Li, Y.; Xu, Z.; Pan, W.; Zhao, Z.; Cushing, M.; Wang, F.; Yang, H. S.
abstract: BackgroundLaboratory medicine underpins clinical decision-making across nearly every care setting. Clinical laboratory errors and delays can compromise diagnostic reliability and patient care. However, laboratory quality and operational data are commonly reviewed through separate manual workflows, limiting timely recognition of emerging problems across complementary data sources. MethodsWe developed and evaluated LabARIA (Laboratory Agentic Reasoning and Integrative Analytics), a multi-agent AI system for coordinated surveillance of specimen workflows, analytical quality control, and laboratory operations. We conducted a single-center retrospective system development and evaluation at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center using laboratory data collected from May 1 through June 18, 2026, including 177,480 specimen-panel records, 75,103 internal quality-control (IQC) measurements, 633 proficiency-testing challenges, and 422 recalibration or maintenance actions. Forecasting agents were evaluated using patient-result streams with controlled perturbations, and synthetic staffing and inventory data. We assessed specimen rejection, cancellation, and turnaround-time patterns; warning recall and lead time before documented laboratory actions; assay-specific patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC) performance; and exploratory operational forecasting discrimination. FindingsLabARIA characterized specimen and workflow patterns across clinical units and time periods, including hemolysis-related potassium rejections in the intensive care unit during early morning hours (49 of 367 tests [13.3%]). For analytical quality monitoring, the IQC agent generated warnings before 407 of 422 recorded QC actions (recall, 0.964 [95% CI, 0.942-0.978]), with a median lead time of 5.40 days (95% CI, 3.75-6.07). PBRTQC agent selected different monitoring strategies across 35 analytes. In a separate analysis, adding PBRTQC increased action recall from 0.964 to 0.993 (95% CI, 0.979-0.998). A dashboard presented tiered alerts for human review, and an accompanying chatbot supported interactive exploration of the summaries. For the operational forecasting module, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 7-day inventory and staffing risk forecasting were 0.800 (95% CI, 0.696-0.881) and 0.877 (95% CI, 0.778-0.950), respectively. InterpretationLabARIA demonstrated the feasibility of coordinating laboratory quality surveillance across heterogeneous data sources, providing a foundation for intelligent clinical laboratories. Prospective studies are warranted to determine whether this approach improves monitoring beyond conventional methods, supports laboratory decisions, and benefits patient care without excessive alert burden. FundingNo external funding. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed and arXiv for studies published between Jan 1, 2016, and Nov 1, 2026, without language restrictions, using ("clinical laboratory" OR "clinical laboratories" OR "laboratory medicine") AND ("artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning" OR "large language model" OR "large language models" OR "agentic AI" OR "multi-agent" OR "multiagent" OR "quality control" OR "laboratory operations"). We included studies addressing laboratory quality monitoring or operations and excluded those focused solely on disease diagnosis or treatment selection. Reliable clinical laboratory services are essential to patient care, yet quality and operational surveillance often relies on manual and retrospective review of data distributed across separate systems, placing substantial burdens on laboratory personnel and contributing to reactive responses to emerging problems. Although laboratory automation has advanced, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning applications in clinical laboratories have generally focused on narrowly defined tasks, such as identifying preanalytical errors, supporting test interpretation, and improving test utilization. Existing approaches typically rely on predefined rules, descriptive dashboards, or task-specific analytical models rather than coordinated surveillance across laboratory workflows. We identified no published study that had developed and evaluated an integrated agentic AI system for laboratory-wide quality and operational surveillance. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first study to develop and evaluate a multi-agent AI system for coordinated laboratory-wide quality and operational surveillance. We developed LabARIA to coordinate specialized agents across specimen workflows, analytical quality monitoring, and laboratory operations, integrating their findings into an interactive dashboard with prioritized alerts, supporting measurements, and recommended follow-up checks for laboratory personnel. Rather than providing descriptive summaries alone, the system brings together complementary analytical findings to support the identification and prioritization of emerging concerns. Using real-world clinical laboratory records, we assessed monitoring performance against documented laboratory actions and established quality-control methods, demonstrating early warnings and complementary warning coverage. We also explored operational risk forecasting using synthetic data. Together, these evaluations provide a practical approach for assessing agentic AI in clinical laboratories. Implications of all the available evidenceOur findings suggest that agentic AI could help advance clinical laboratory quality surveillance from fragmented and reactive review toward more coordinated and proactive monitoring. By integrating complementary monitoring functions and presenting prioritized findings with supporting evidence, agentic systems offer a potential approach to helping laboratory personnel identify emerging concerns and focus their investigations. This study advances agentic laboratory surveillance from concept to implementation and evaluation, representing a step toward intelligent clinical laboratories in which AI supports coordinated quality monitoring and human decision-making.

infographic.key_insight: In retrospective evaluation, LabARIA coordinated laboratory surveillance agents and generated quality-control warnings before 96.4% of recorded laboratory actions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Integrated monitoring could help laboratory teams identify specimen, workflow, and analytical quality issues for human review, though patient-care benefits remain unproven.
method: Combined multi-agent analysis of specimen workflows, internal quality control, and laboratory operations.
Selected patient-based real-time quality-control strategies across 35 analytes.
Presented tiered alerts and interactive summaries through a dashboard and chatbot.
infographic.evidence_signal: Single-center evaluation included 177,480 specimen-panel records and 75,103 internal quality-control measurements; warnings preceded 407 of 422 recorded actions, with a median lead time of 5.40 days.
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective action-based recall does not establish prospective usefulness or false-alert burden; operational forecasting also used controlled perturbations and synthetic staffing and inventory data.
infographic.paper_title: LabARIA: A Multi-Agent System for Integrative Analytics in Clinical Laboratories

title: Hard to Halt: Automation Bias in Agent-Driven Sequencing Prior Authorization Workflows
authors: Nie, M.; Chung, W.; Waxler, J.; Lee, M.; Weng, C.; Lewis, R.; Ahimaz, P.; Wang, K.; Liu, C.
abstract: PurposePrior authorization (PA) for exome or genome sequencing (ES/GS) is a time-consuming process that impedes timely rare disease diagnosis. Large language model (LLM)-based browser agents offer potential for automating these workflows, but their clinical reliability remains uncharacterized. MethodsWe built a sandbox with a simulated ES/GS payer portal and a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) of 836 patient profiles, including compliant profiles and deficient profiles with designed issues. Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, and Claude Opus 4.5 were evaluated on task completion, form accuracy, and appropriate withholding. Two replication experiments were run on 100 profiles to assess run-to-run variability of agent performance. ResultsGemini 3 Pro (95.5%) and Claude Opus 4.5 (93.7%) completed far more tasks than Gemini 3 Flash (56.1%), consistently across runs. In the first run, all models rarely withheld deficient profiles for the correct reason (Gemini 3 Pro 0%, Gemini 3 Flash 17.3%, Claude Opus 4.5 5.2%). Replication revealed substantial variability: Gemini 3 Pros correct withholding rose to 28.8-36.8%, and only 18.0-48.0% of tasks yielded identical outcomes across all three runs. Without agentic scaffolding, Gemini 3 Pro flagged designed issues in 91.3% of deficient profiles but also halted on all compliant profiles. ConclusionCurrent LLM-based browser agents show a systematic bias toward form submission. A modular, multi-agent architecture with human supervision may be warranted for safe clinical deployment.

infographic.key_insight: High task completion did not ensure appropriate withholding: browser agents often submitted sequencing prior authorizations despite designed deficiencies.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automating exome/genome sequencing prior authorization could reduce administrative burden, but unreliable withholding raises concerns about unsupervised use.
method: Built a simulated payer portal and synthetic EHR containing 836 compliant or deliberately deficient patient profiles.
Evaluated Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, and Claude Opus 4.5 for task completion, form accuracy, and appropriate withholding.
Ran two replication experiments on 100 profiles to assess run-to-run variability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Initial task completion ranged from 56.1% to 95.5%, while correct withholding on deficient profiles ranged from 0% to 17.3%; only 18.0–48.0% of tasks had identical outcomes across three runs.
infographic.watch_item: Synthetic sandbox results do not establish real-world safety; submission bias and run-to-run variability warrant human oversight before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Hard to Halt: Automation Bias in Agent-Driven Sequencing Prior Authorization Workflows

title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift
authors: Ziyao Mou, Andrea Wynn, Eric Nalisnick
abstract: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyaoMou/L2D-Expert-Drift.

infographic.key_insight: EDA-L2D uses recent expert outcomes to adapt when an AI system defers decisions as human reliability changes over time.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Adaptive deferral could support medical AI workflows when clinician performance fluctuates, though clinical benefit is not established by the abstract.
method: Model temporal changes in expert reliability.
Condition the deferral head on recent expert outcomes using a sequence model.
Adapt decision allocation between AI and human experts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments spanning image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection report better system performance and deferral decisions than prior L2D methods, including under irregular reliability shifts.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment would require timely, reliable feedback on expert outcomes; the abstract does not establish prospective clinical safety.
infographic.paper_title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift

title: Integrating Histopathology Foundation Models and PRAME Immunohistochemistry in Melanoma Diagnosis
authors: Gellrich, F. F.; Kistner, A.; Guenther, C.; Hufnagel, C.; Hobelsberger, S.; Laske, J.; Beissert, S.; Aust, D.; Baretton, G.; Reidow, N.; Sergon, M.; Kather, J. N.; Ghaffari Laleh, N.
abstract: BackgroundThe histopathological diagnosis of challenging melanocytic lesions remains limited by substantial interobserver variability. Although computational pathology foundation models demonstrated promising diagnostic performance, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in terms of established criteria. ObjectiveWe evaluated a diagnostic framework combining foundation-model-based whole-slide image analysis, automated prediction of morphological features, and manually assessed PRAME immunohistochemistry. MethodsUsing the Virchow2 foundation model and STAMP framework, we analyzed a retrospective cohort of 1,000 melanocytic lesions undergoing PRAME immunohistochemistry. Models were trained on 800 cases and evaluated on a temporally held-out test cohort of 200 cases. ResultsThe slide-level malignancy classifier achieved a test AUROC of 0.970 (AUPRC 0.984). Separate models predicted established histopathological criteria with high discrimination, including ulceration (AUROC 0.991) and dermal mitoses (AUROC 0.966). In contrast, predicting PRAME expression from H&E images alone showed lower performance (AUROC 0.776-0.780 for PRAME scores 4 and 0). An integrated model combining the slide-level malignancy score, AI-predicted morphological features, and manual PRAME status achieved an AUROC of 0.972 (AUPRC 0.975), comparable to the standalone classifier. In multivariable analysis, PRAME score 4 versus 0 was strongly associated with malignancy (adjusted OR 35.04, 95% CI 17.39-74.62). ConclusionsThese findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining foundation-model-based histopathological analysis with established morphological criteria and PRAME immunohistochemistry. Although the integrated framework did not substantially improve overall discrimination, it provides a structured approach for incorporating complementary histopathological and immunohistochemical information into AI-assisted assessment of melanocytic lesions. Key PointsO_ST_ABSWhy was the study undertaken?C_ST_ABSDeep learning models in histopathology often lack diagnostic transparency. Existing frameworks rarely incorporate established morphological criteria or manually assessed findings, such as PRAME immunohistochemistry, in the evaluation of challenging melanocytic lesions. What does this study add?We evaluated a framework combining foundation-model-based whole-slide analysis with AI-predicted morphological features and manual PRAME status. Although overall diagnostic performance was comparable to the standalone model, integrating these criteria as statistically significant predictors aligns the algorithmic output with established histopathological parameters. What are the implications of this study for disease understanding and/or clinical care?This study demonstrates the feasibility of combining computational models with standard histopathological workflows. Correlating algorithmic predictions with established criteria facilitates potential clinical applications, including automated case triaging and diagnostic decision support. Plain Language SummaryDiagnosing melanoma, a type of skin cancer, under a microscope can be challenging. In difficult cases, doctors may sometimes reach different conclusions. Artificial intelligence (AI) computer programs can accurately analyze digitized tissue samples, but they often function as "black boxes," making it difficult for doctors to understand how the AI reached its conclusion. In this study, we tested an AI system on 1,000 skin samples. Instead of relying solely on the AI to provide a final diagnosis, we combined its analysis with specific microscopic features that doctors routinely look for, alongside the results of a special laboratory test called PRAME. We found that the AI system was highly accurate in identifying melanoma. While combining the AI with the specific tissue features and the PRAME test did not further increase the overall accuracy, it successfully aligned the computers output with established medical standards. This approach demonstrates that advanced computer models can be integrated with traditional laboratory tests. By linking AI results to familiar medical criteria, the systems output becomes more transparent for physicians, which could help doctors evaluate difficult skin tissue samples more efficiently in the future.

infographic.key_insight: Combining AI slide analysis, predicted morphology, and manually assessed PRAME staining achieved similar malignancy discrimination to AI slide analysis alone.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could help connect AI predictions with established pathological findings when assessing challenging melanocytic lesions.
method: Analyzed whole-slide images using the Virchow2 foundation model and STAMP framework.
Trained models to classify malignancy and predict established morphological features.
Integrated AI scores and predicted features with manually assessed PRAME status.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a retrospective cohort of 1,000 lesions, models trained on 800 cases achieved test AUROCs of 0.970 for standalone classification and 0.972 for the integrated model on 200 temporally held-out cases.
infographic.watch_item: The integrated model did not substantially improve discrimination; external and prospective validation are needed before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Integrating Histopathology Foundation Models and PRAME Immunohistochemistry in Melanoma Diagnosis

title: Multimodal AI in Healthcare: Review of Vision-Language Foundation Models for Real-World Medical Applications
authors: Taha Razzaq, Murtaza Taj, Asim Iqbal
abstract: The emergence of foundation models has marked a transformative shift in AI, enabling robust generalization across diverse downstream tasks through putative zero-shot learning. Large Language Models and Vision Language Models have demonstrated strong capabilities in tasks such as image interpretation, report generation, and question answering by effectively learning from multimodal data-images paired with associated text often with minimal supervision. In the healthcare domain, this ability to align visual and textual information reduces the reliance on extensive manual annotations, as models can leverage existing clinical reports and imaging data to learn meaningful representations. This integration holds promise for improving diagnostic support, treatment planning, and overall patient care, even in data constrained settings. In this review, we provide a definitive taxonomy of the medical VLM landscape, tracing the evolution from early Contrastive Alignment and Generative MLLMs to the cutting edge frontiers of Dense Pixel Grounding, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), and Reasoning Incentivized (RL) architectures. We critically examine the "medical bottleneck" identifying the persistent challenges of data scarcity, the "hallucination" risks in generative diagnostics, the computational strain of 3D volumetric processing, and the lack of standardized, clinically grounded evaluation metrics.

infographic.key_insight: This review maps medical vision-language models from contrastive alignment and generative systems to pixel grounding, mixture-of-experts, and reinforcement-learning-based reasoning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Aligning medical images with clinical text could support image interpretation, report generation, and question answering while reducing reliance on manual annotations.
method: Reviews foundation models that learn from paired images and text.
Organizes medical vision-language architectures into a taxonomy.
Examines data, reliability, computational, and evaluation challenges.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a review rather than a clinical validation study and reports no dataset sizes or quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Hallucinated outputs and a lack of standardized, clinically grounded evaluation limit confidence in real-world deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Multimodal AI in Healthcare: Review of Vision-Language Foundation Models for Real-World Medical Applications

title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
authors: Zhiyu Liu, Xinyu Yang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.

infographic.key_insight: A query-only LLM audit closely reproduced clinical prediction models and detected 96% of planted flaws, but its additional problem reports and discoveries required independent verification.
infographic.clinical_relevance: LLM audits may help inspect opaque clinical prediction tools, but these results do not establish clinical safety or improved patient outcomes.
method: Trained four model types on International Stroke Trial data for two outcomes.
Mixed 24 models with planted flaws and 8 clean models; GPT-6 Astra audited each three times using prediction queries only.
Applied pre-specified automated judging rules and tested unexpected relationships in later-randomised patients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Surrogates achieved mean log-odds R² of 0.976; the LLM detected 69/72 planted flaws across audit runs (96%; 95% CI 80–99%), while a purpose-written script detected all 24 flawed models.
infographic.watch_item: Of 1,089 checkable problem reports, 60% failed the pre-specified average-behaviour check; post hoc analysis found most were real but small steps, while 15% were absent from the model.
infographic.paper_title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws

title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
authors: Una Suman Kumar Patro, Sibangi Subhadarsani, Narendra Badam
abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.

infographic.key_insight: Combining structured EHR features, clinical-text embeddings, and knowledge-grounded entity extraction improved sensitivity for 30-day diabetic readmission prediction, but slightly reduced AUROC.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could help identify more patients who are later readmitted, though its low specificity raises concerns about false-positive alerts.
method: Fuse engineered EHR features with 32 compressed Bio_ClinicalBERT embedding components.
Extract symbolic entities using a clinical language model, hybrid retrieval, re-ranking, and negation auditing.
Predict readmission with cost-sensitive XGBoost and a threshold calibrated using Youden’s J.
infographic.evidence_signal: With a patient-grouped 80/20 split and 20,153 held-out encounters, sensitivity rose from 0.5839 to 0.6667 and Brier score improved from 0.1080 to 0.0977, while AUROC fell from 0.6477 to 0.6375.
infographic.watch_item: External and prospective validation are needed; performance on a separate 500-note Hinglish benchmark does not establish real-world multilingual clinical utility.
infographic.paper_title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction

title: Adversarial Robustness of Capsule Networks for Medical Image Classification
authors: Srinivasan, A.; Sritharan, D. V.; Chadha, S.; Fu, D.; Hossain, J. O.; Breuer, G. A.; Aneja, S.
abstract: PurposeDeep learning models are increasingly being used in medical diagnostics, but their vulnerability to adversarial perturbations raises concerns about their reliability in clinical applications. Capsule networks (CapsNets) are a promising architecture for medical imaging tasks, given their ability to model spatial relationships and train with smaller amounts of data. Although previous studies have focused on adversarial training approaches to improve robustness, exploring alternative architectures is an underexplored direction for combating poor adversarial stability. Prior work has suggested that CapsNets may exhibit improved robustness to adversarial perturbations compared to convolutional neural networks (CNNs), but performance on adversarial images has not been studied systematically in clinical environments. We evaluated the robustness of CapsNets compared to CNNs and vision transformers (ViTs) across multiple medical image classification tasks. MethodsWe trained two CNNs (ResNet-18 and ResNet-50), one ViT (MedViT), and two CapsNets (DR-CapsNet and BP-CapsNet) on four distinct medical imaging datasets (PneumoniaMNIST, BreastMNIST, NoduleMNIST3D, and BloodMNIST) and one natural image dataset (MNIST). Models were evaluated on adversarial examples generated by projected gradient descent, fast gradient sign method, AutoAttack, Carlini & Wagner, and black-box transfer attacks. Models also underwent PGD adversarial fine-tuning to assess whether architectural differences persisted after adversarial training. Interpretability experiments, including latent space and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) analyses, were conducted to better understand model stability on adversarial inputs. ResultsUnder conventional training, CapsNets demonstrated superior robustness under adversarial perturbations compared to CNNs and ViTs across all medical imaging datasets and the natural image dataset. Latent space and Grad-CAM visualizations revealed that CapsNets maintained more consistent feature representations and attention maps after adversarial perturbations compared to CNNs and ViTs, suggesting that advantages in CapsNet robustness are supported, at least in part, by more stable feature encodings. PGD adversarial fine-tuning improved robustness across models, with MedViT exhibiting the largest gains and thereby narrowing the performance gap. ConclusionCapsNets exhibit advantages in adversarial robustness over CNN- and ViT-based models on medical imaging tasks. These findings suggest that capsule-based architectures may be a promising direction for robust medical image classification. Future work should validate CapsNet robustness across more complex medical imaging tasks, independent external datasets, and broader sources of real-world imaging variability.

infographic.key_insight: Under conventional training, capsule networks showed greater adversarial robustness than the tested CNNs and vision transformer across all five datasets.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Capsule networks may help improve medical image classifier reliability under adversarial perturbations, but clinical safety and effectiveness remain unestablished.
method: Compared two capsule networks, ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and MedViT.
Evaluated five adversarial attack approaches and conducted PGD adversarial fine-tuning.
Used latent-space and Grad-CAM analyses to examine representation stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered four medical imaging datasets and MNIST; visualizations suggested more stable capsule-network representations and attention maps after perturbation.
infographic.watch_item: The supplied abstract is incomplete and provides no numerical effect sizes or results after adversarial fine-tuning.
infographic.paper_title: Adversarial Robustness of Capsule Networks for Medical Image Classification

title: Multi-institutional grading of Barrett's esophagus dysplasia without stain normalization using a pathology foundation model and multiple instance learning
authors: Amirali Khosravi, Jaidip M. Jagtap, D. Chamil Codipilly, Catherine E. Hagen, Jason T. Lewis, Rickey E. Carter
abstract: Barrett's esophagus dysplasia grading suffers substantial inter-observer variability, particularly for low-grade dysplasia, complicating clinical decision-making. We conducted a retrospective multi-institutional diagnostic accuracy study of a foundation model-based deep learning system for dysplasia grading, using 969 H\&E-stained whole slide images from four institutions. Patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identified diagnostically relevant regions, followed by attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification as non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus (NDBE), low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia. On a held-out test set (n = 130), macro-averaged AUC was 0.96 (95\% CI 0.93--0.98). For binary dysplasia detection, sensitivity was 98\% (80/82) and specificity 81\% (39/48), with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.030 and quadratic-weighted \kap{} of 0.83 against expert consensus. No high-grade dysplasia case was misclassified as NDBE. Performance was consistent across institutions without stain normalization, indicating that stain-robust foundation-model representations may remove the site-specific preprocessing that has constrained prior systems to institution-specific deployment.

infographic.key_insight: A pathology foundation model combined with multiple instance learning graded Barrett’s esophagus dysplasia across institutions without stain normalization, achieving a macro-averaged AUC of 0.96.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more consistent dysplasia grading, where pathologist disagreement can complicate clinical decisions.
method: Retrospective study of 969 H&E-stained whole-slide images from four institutions.
Patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identified diagnostically relevant regions.
Attribute-aware multiple instance learning classified slides as non-dysplastic Barrett’s esophagus, low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 130 held-out slides, macro-averaged AUC was 0.96 (95% CI 0.93–0.98); binary dysplasia detection achieved 98% sensitivity and 81% specificity, with no high-grade case classified as non-dysplastic.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective validation in additional institutions and clinical workflows is needed before routine deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-institutional grading of Barrett's esophagus dysplasia without stain normalization using a pathology foundation model and multiple instance learning

title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
authors: Eleftherios Tzanis, Michail E. Klontzas
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

infographic.key_insight: System 1 agents select tools and arguments without generating text, achieving high accuracy with no invented content observed in evaluated calls.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Local tool execution could support analysis of sensitive clinical data without sending requests to cloud LLMs, though clinical safety remains unestablished.
method: A deterministic compiler converts tool schemas and requests into multiple-choice questions.
Answer options come from the request and tool schema.
A one-pass decision model selects answers to construct tool calls.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best agent achieved 97.0% correct tool selection or decline versus 95.2% for the best local LLM setting, filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values, and produced no invented call content.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish real-world clinical safety; deployment needs validation on local tools, workflows, and data.
infographic.paper_title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI

title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
authors: Huixin Zhan, Jason H. Moore
abstract: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

infographic.key_insight: An uncertainty-conditioned AI framework converts genomic predictions into traceable, graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, with uncertainty explicitly shaping hypothesis breadth.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support research into variant–phenotype links, but the abstract does not establish patient-level diagnostic utility.
method: Combine sequence predictions and calibrated uncertainty with biomedical knowledge graphs.
Score gene–disease–phenotype paths using a learned energy function and uncertainty-dependent temperature.
Aggregate path probabilities into phenotype hypotheses without patient-level phenotype supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype entropy correlated with upstream uncertainty (Spearman 0.951 and 0.878); under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeded trained DistMult on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123).
infographic.watch_item: The gene hold-out advantage was driven mainly by three genes with many variants and is not established across all genes.
infographic.paper_title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs

title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
authors: Yufan Wang, Rui Yang, Yi Lin, Chunhua Weng, Yifan Peng
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

infographic.key_insight: DiagTrace evaluates how LLMs seek information to reconstruct documented diagnostic trajectories, rather than judging only their final diagnoses.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark tests incremental evidence gathering, an aspect of diagnostic reasoning missed when all patient information is provided upfront.
method: Build source-grounded cases from PubMed Central case reports.
Provide an initial presentation, event bank, clinical course, and diagnostic references.
Evaluate interactive information seeking for clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency.
infographic.evidence_signal: DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties; evaluation of four LLMs on 225 cases revealed trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.
infographic.watch_item: Alignment with published case-report trajectories does not establish diagnostic safety or effectiveness in real-world patient care.
infographic.paper_title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making

title: Verifiable Logic in Medical LLMs: A Critical Review of Agentic Clinical Reasoning Optimization and Neuro-Symbolic Grounding
authors: Youssef ElNahas, Adel Ammar, Soumaya Chaffar, Wadii Boulila
abstract: Clinical large language models are usually judged by whether the final answer is right. Yet a model can reach a fluent, plausible output through invalid reasoning that static benchmarks do not detect, and confident hallucination, causally invalid inference, and spurious demographic shortcuts can pass conventional evaluation. This critical review covers four paradigms in turn: how clinical hallucination arises and why static metrics miss it; the agentic hallucination cascade, in which multi-agent and tool-augmented systems propagate and amplify early reasoning errors; process reward modeling as step-level supervision; and neuro-symbolic grounding, in which formal logic engines, ontology reasoners, and knowledge graphs place verifiable constraints on neural output. Within their encoded domains, systems with symbolic veto layers offer guarantees that hold relative to their encoded knowledge, and they report large gains on the safety measures they use. These results come from single studies, mostly in simulated or small-sample settings, and are not directly comparable with neural baselines. Process reward models remain bounded by the statistics of their training data. We propose a conceptual framework that maps each agentic failure mode to a symbolic intervention point, and we argue that clinical AI safety depends substantially on system architecture. Because current regulation emphasizes performance and does not require verification of reasoning steps, we argue that responsible certification should also audit reasoning trajectories alongside accuracy on static benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: Clinical AI safety requires checking reasoning processes, not just final answers, with symbolic constraints offering safeguards within their encoded domains.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Auditing reasoning trajectories may help detect plausible but invalid clinical outputs that accuracy benchmarks miss.
method: Critically reviews hallucination, agentic error cascades, process reward modeling, and neuro-symbolic grounding.
Proposes a conceptual framework linking agentic failure modes to symbolic intervention points.
Argues for certification that audits reasoning alongside benchmark accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported safety gains come from individual studies, mostly in simulated or small-sample settings, and are not directly comparable with neural baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Symbolic guarantees depend on the encoded knowledge and do not establish safety beyond that scope.
infographic.paper_title: Verifiable Logic in Medical LLMs: A Critical Review of Agentic Clinical Reasoning Optimization and Neuro-Symbolic Grounding

title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
authors: Guanqiao Chen, Wei Jiang, Shu Zhang, Qian Lin, Guanxu Yu, Siran Li
abstract: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

infographic.key_insight: A correct final diagnosis can mask potentially harmful intermediate decisions, and correcting an error can introduce new risks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Clinical AI evaluation should assess the safety of tests, treatments and disposition decisions throughout a case—not just diagnostic accuracy.
method: Replayed admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, exposing AI systems only to evidence available at each stage.
Scored each decision separately for potential harm and clinical validity, using an LLM judge calibrated against physician review.
Branched trajectories at the first actionable error to compare error repair and new risks after corrective feedback.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 300 cases from three sources, 55.2% of hospital trajectories with acceptable final diagnoses included moderate or severe potential harm; structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, but new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% versus 19.7%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: These retrospective audits measured potential harm rather than observed patient injury, and physician calibration covered a stratified sample.
infographic.paper_title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm

title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
authors: The InclusionMed Collaboration
abstract: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

infographic.key_insight: Medical AI rankings varied by healthcare role and capability, showing why one overall score cannot capture performance across healthcare needs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Context-specific evaluation can inform model selection for healthcare tasks, but these benchmark results do not establish clinical safety or effectiveness.
method: Organized benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities.
Selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction, then added a private diagnostic reasoning benchmark.
Evaluated frontier language models and aggregated results into an overall Index and role- and capability-specific scores.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five benchmarks, overall Index scores ranged from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100; all ten highest-ranked models scored higher on patient communication than clinical decision-making.
infographic.watch_item: The Atlas covers only three of nine role–capability cells, limiting conclusions about performance across diverse healthcare needs.
infographic.paper_title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare

title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models
authors: Shengjie Niu, Yeheng Ge, Jian Huang
abstract: Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large language model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text and medical question-answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a unified statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.

infographic.key_insight: A unified statistical framework combines passage-level signals to audit whether individual documents or collections were used to train an LLM.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For medical AI, this approach could support audits of training-data provenance and potential benchmark contamination involving medical question-answer records.
method: Combine complementary chunk-level membership evidence using Cauchy combination to score documents.
Use calibrated document-level p-values to assess training use across a target collection.
Apply multiple testing to identify suspicious documents with false discovery rate control.
infographic.evidence_signal: Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic evaluated audits of pre-training and fine-tuning data; the abstract reports effectiveness and reliability without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Statistical guarantees depend on stated exchangeability conditions, which require scrutiny before applying the framework to new medical datasets.
infographic.paper_title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models

title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Missing Covariates: An Empirical Evaluation with Applications to Alzheimer's Disease Research
authors: Yiqing Pan, Sharon X. Xie, Shujie Ma, Angela L. Jefferson, Panpan Zhang
abstract: Missing data are common in biomedical research, particularly when biomarkers are costly or require invasive procedures to obtain, such as cerebrospinal fluid measures in Alzheimer's disease. Although a wide range of missing data methods exists, from traditional statistical approaches to modern machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, their comparative performance under different missingness mechanisms remains insufficiently understood. In this study, we provide an empirical evaluation of eight methods for handling missing covariates, including complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, ML-based techniques, and DL frameworks such as multilayer perceptrons, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks. We summarize their conceptual foundations, practical implementation considerations, strengths, and limitations. Through extensive simulations, we assess estimation bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, confidence interval coverage, and computational burden across different missingness mechanisms and proportions. An application to the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project further illustrates the implications of different methods for regression analysis in a real-world biomedical setting. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for method selection and highlight remaining challenges that warrant future investigation.

infographic.key_insight: This study compares eight approaches to missing covariates, from traditional statistics to deep learning, to inform method selection in Alzheimer’s disease research.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Handling missing biomarkers appropriately matters for interpreting Alzheimer’s research, especially when measurements are costly or invasive to obtain.
method: Compare complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, and machine learning methods.
Evaluate deep learning frameworks including multilayer perceptrons, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks.
Assess regression estimates across missingness mechanisms and proportions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations assess bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, confidence interval coverage, and computational burden, alongside an application to the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no comparative results, so it does not establish a best-performing method.
infographic.paper_title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Missing Covariates: An Empirical Evaluation with Applications to Alzheimer's Disease Research

title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
authors: Tiancheng Bao, Riga Wu, Jan Wienhold, Sebastian Billig, Patrick Winnersbach, Hsuan-Chih Chen
abstract: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

infographic.key_insight: Decision2Care performed clinical work-ups without generating text, recording candidate actions, probabilities, and execution rules for audit.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Auditable action records could help clinicians review how an AI assessment evolved, though clinical deployment requires further validation.
method: Assigns probabilities to permitted electronic health record actions.
Uses fixed rules to execute the highest-probability action.
Tracks diagnostic options at each step and applies the same decision approach to treatment selection.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 546 emergency admissions covering 12 diseases, diagnostic accuracy was 86.5% versus MIRA-v2’s 86.1%, with a median work-up time of 2.2 seconds versus 92–100 seconds.
infographic.watch_item: This records-based evaluation does not establish prospective clinical safety; four errors in the highest-confidence diagnoses were traced to individual imaging reports.
infographic.paper_title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
